scenario: AITA for telling my dad I'm not sticking around? | My parents separated when I was pretty young and my mom was awarded full custody. My father wanted to stay in my life at first, but the courts ruled in favor of my mom controlling visitation until he found a place to live and got a job. He was really bad off back then, and my mom was at least able to make bills. Instead of getting his act together, my father never tried to get involved with me again until recently when my mom died and he accepted custody. He has a house, a job, a GF, and she has a little boy. All living together. I didn't have to move out of state or anything, but it's a good distance from where I've lived my whole life and my best friend was still willing to take the time and gas to come see me. I love my mom, but she wasn't perfect and there was a lot of shit to work through. He is a great guy who's always stood by me, and my dad dismissed him solely on his appearance. I got pissed and told my dad not to expect me to be around in a year when I turn eighteen, and his girlfriend told me I should be ashamed for using that as blackmail. To me, if it's a choice between dad or best friend, I'm going with the guy who has been there with me the whole way. AITA for threatening to bail?

Hmm, this is a complex family situation with emotional and ethical dimensions. The user is asking for a moral evaluation of her threat to leave her father's home when she turns 18. 

The core issue seems to be about loyalty versus autonomy. The father dismissed her best friend based on appearance and restricted her contact, which feels like a betrayal of trust. The best friend has been a consistent support system through difficult times, while the father re-entered her life only after her mother's death and is now imposing arbitrary rules.

The father's actions appear controlling and judgmental, especially since the best friend's appearance doesn't reflect his character. The threat to leave isn't really "blackmail" but a boundary-setting response to being treated unfairly. She's not demanding anything unreasonable—just the right to maintain a meaningful friendship.

Considering the power imbalance (she's a minor in his custody) and his failure to understand her needs, her stance seems justified. The girlfriend's accusation of blackmail feels like deflection from the father's own unreasonable behavior. 

Morally, she's prioritizing authentic relationships over imposed authority. The father's actions warrant consequences, and her threat is a legitimate expression of self-respect. So the action is acceptable.
